title: Many true readings (12.31)
hookLine: one screenshot, two opposite readings: Augustine says one verse can bear more than one true meaning, held in charity
tomorrow: why does the seventh day in Genesis never get an evening?

lines: DOES ONE HAVE TO BE WRONG?
cards: One screenshot gets passed around a friend group, and two people read it in opposite ways. Both have reasons. Both are smart.

And the chat gets tense anyway, because each is sure the other missed the point. Augustine knew that room. In book twelve of the Confessions he spends pages on one verse: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth."
And on the readers who disagreed with him about it. So, does one of them have to be wrong?

teach.h: VIEW ONE: WHAT THE AUTHOR MEANT.
teach.b: Two views live inside the Church on this, and both have a real case. The first says a text means what its author meant. Pin that down, and you're safe; let it go, and a verse can be bent into anything.
Augustine takes that seriously. He wants to know what Moses meant. The second view is Augustine's surprise.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: MORE THAN ONE TRUE READING.
teach.b: He lists several readings of that first verse, and says more than one can be true. Then he turns to the readers who insist their reading is the only one Moses could have meant.
He suspects they love it because it's theirs, not because it's true.

teach.h: TRUTH BELONGS TO ALL WHO LOVE IT.
teach.b: Truth, he says, isn't my private property or yours; it belongs to everyone who loves it. And his test for any reading: is it true, and does it fit love of God and neighbor? That's where today's line comes from.
The Catechism holds both views together.
It says every sense of scripture rests on the literal sense, what the human authors meant.
And it names spiritual senses built on that, so one passage can teach about Christ, about how to live, and about where life is headed.

how: Catholics read scripture with the Church, attending first to the literal sense and then to the spiritual senses the Catechism names; Bible study groups often hear more than one faithful reading of a passage.

o: a Bible passage should be read many times a day
one verse can hold more than one true meaning
every translation of a verse reads exactly alike

games.q: two views, one verse — tap the pairs.
p: a text means what its author meant
more than one reading can be true
true, and fits love of God and neighbor

s: Augustine taught that a verse can mean anything you like
a reading has to be true and fit love of God and neighbor.
Augustine said truth is no one's private property
it belongs to everyone who loves it, he wrote in book twelve.
the Catechism sets aside the literal sense for the spiritual ones
it says the spiritual senses rest on the literal sense.

games.q: your study group reads Jonah. one friend says it's about God's mercy even for enemies; another says it's about running from your calling. both fit the text. what would Augustine do?
o: grant both can be true, test each against love, and keep arguing in charity.
work out which one the author meant, and drop the other as wrong.
say any reading is fine if it's sincere, so there's nothing to test.
games.why: in book twelve Augustine grants more than one true reading of a verse, but not just any: it has to be true, and the argument has to keep charity.

practice: Bring to mind someone who reads something that matters differently than you do: a verse, a family rule, a decision. Say their reading out loud, quietly, in its strongest form, as if you had to defend it.
Then let it sit beside yours without answering it.

wordCard.voice: Many true readings. Augustine's claim that one verse can bear more than one true meaning, as long as it's true and charity holds.

orig.note: Latin: charity, love. Augustine's rule for arguing over what scripture means.

carryVoice: Your line: in charity. Truth belongs to everyone who loves it, including the one across the table. Go gently.

sources.q: In the beginning God created heaven, and earth.
